p: After studying this chapter, you should be able to do the following.
list: State what precautions to take before transporting pesticides.
Summarize what the label says about legally disposing of unwanted pesticides.
List the steps to take to restrict access to pesticides.
Explain how to create a safe and secure storage area.
Describe how to properly store pesticides.
Discuss how to reduce the amounts stored by controlling inventory.
Explain how to maintain the integrity of pesticide containers.

p: This chapter discusses safety and security issues that may arise when pesticides are moved or stored.
Serious accidents involving pesticides are **more likely to occur while they are in transit**.
Securing pesticides in a vehicle or in storage is a critical step to **prevent vandalism or theft** of product.
You can reduce pesticide transport and storage problems by being aware of conditions that lead to increased security risks.
Every pesticide applicator should understand the hazards of transporting pesticides and the procedures for minimizing those risks.
Pesticides are moved by manufacturers to distributors, from retailers to end users, and from storage sites to job sites.
Transportation-related accidents can happen at **any point in the distribution chain**, from the manufacturer to the job site.
Your **first line of defense** is recognizing how to prevent these transportation mishaps.
When accidents occur, the **timing of your response** could determine the size of the spill.

figures.title: Sign: Danger, Peligro. Fire will cause toxic fumes. Pesticide storage area. All unauthorized persons keep out. Keep door locked when not in use.

questions.q: According to the manual, when are serious accidents involving pesticides more likely to occur?
choices: While the pesticides are in storage
While the pesticides are in transit
While the pesticides are being mixed
While the pesticides are being disposed of
questions.why: Serious accidents are more likely to occur while pesticides are in transit.

questions.q: What does the manual call your first line of defense against transportation accidents?
choices: Recognizing how to prevent these transportation mishaps
questions.why: Your first line of defense is recognizing how to prevent these transportation mishaps.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT named as a point where pesticides are moved in the distribution chain?
questions.why: The manual names manufacturers to distributors, retailers to end users, and storage sites to job sites.

questions.q: A tank of pesticide tips over on a truck. According to the manual, what could determine the size of the spill?
questions.why: When accidents occur, the timing of your response could determine the size of the spill.

questions.q: Transportation-related accidents can happen only on public highways, not at other points in the distribution chain.
questions.why: They can happen at any point in the distribution chain, from the manufacturer to the job site.

sections.title: The transport vehicle and securing the load

p: Transport vehicles should be in **good mechanical condition**.
Make sure **brakes, tires, and steering** are in proper working order.
Repair all fluid leaks before putting a truck on the road or leaving the job site.
Regularly inspect application equipment to be transported and used.
Inspect **hoses under pressure for wear and cracks** and **hose clamps for rust**.
Always carry **supplies and replacement parts** to make emergency repairs if a leak should develop while going to and from the job site.
**Never carry liquid pesticides in the passenger area**, because spilled chemicals may cause harmful fumes that can be inhaled.
A pesticide spilled in the cab is difficult to remove and may lead to **long-term inhalation exposure**.
It is best to keep pesticide containers in the **original shipping box**.
Depending on the material, many of these boxes meet the **U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT)** packaging standards to give added protection to the contents.
Try to carry a **minimum amount** of pesticide products on a vehicle at any one time.
Secure and protect pesticide containers against **punctures and impacts** from items packed closely together.
**Enclosed cargo boxes** provide extra security from curious children, thieves, or vandals.
**Never stack pesticide containers higher than the sides of the vehicle.**
Make sure flatbed trucks have **tie-down rings or racks** to simplify the job of securing the load.

figures.title: Secure pesticides while transporting them even for short distances.
Never carry pesticides in the passenger compartment of a vehicle.
Cargo boxes allow for secure transport of pesticides and help prevent theft and vandalism.

questions.q: Which statement about transporting pesticides is true?
choices: Carry pesticides in the passenger compartment to prevent unauthorized access.
Enclosed and lockable cargo boxes offer the greatest protection.
The operator (driver) is not held responsible if a pesticide spill or accident occurs.
questions.why: Enclosed cargo boxes provide extra security, pesticides never go in the passenger area, and the driver is accountable.

questions.q: Why does the manual say never to carry liquid pesticides in the passenger area?
choices: The cab is too warm for pesticides
Spilled chemicals may cause harmful fumes that can be inhaled
questions.why: A spill in the cab can cause harmful fumes and long-term inhalation exposure.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a transport vehicle check named in the manual?
choices: Brakes, tires, and steering in proper working order
Hoses under pressure inspected for wear and cracks
questions.why: The manual lists brakes, tires, steering, fluid leaks, hoses, and hose clamps, nothing about extra tire pressure.

questions.q: You are loading a pickup with jugs of pesticide. The stack would rise above the sides of the bed. What should you do?
choices: Stack them anyway and drive slowly
Do not stack them higher than the sides of the vehicle
Put the extra jugs in the cab
Cover the stack with a tarp
questions.why: Never stack pesticide containers higher than the sides of the vehicle.

questions.q: It is best to move pesticide containers out of their original shipping boxes before transport.
questions.why: It is best to keep them in the original shipping box, which may meet DOT packaging standards.

questions.q: What should flatbed trucks have to simplify the job of securing the load?
questions.why: Flatbed trucks should have tie-down rings or racks.

sections.title: Vehicle operator, SDSs, spill kits, and temperature

p: The person driving the vehicle and/or the owner of the company is **accountable for injuries to people and any pesticide release** into the environment.
The vehicle operator (driver) is the **first person who can contain the spill** and prevent it from spreading.
By the time first responders arrive on the scene, the spill may already be contained.
Therefore, it is important that the driver know **basic emergency response procedures** to contain the spill, **company guidelines**, and **who will notify local, state, and federal authorities**.
Chapter 9, Emergency or Incident Response, explains in detail how to respond to a fire, spill, or leak involving pesticides.

It should be noted that some drivers transporting pesticides regulated as **hazardous materials** will be required to follow **DOT regulations** regarding **commercial driver licenses, placarding, shipping papers, and annual inspections**.
Always carry **product labels and Safety Data Sheets (SDSs)** when transporting pesticides on highways.
The SDS contains critical information for the driver and emergency responders after a pesticide spill.

It lists steps to safely deal with the spill, including the **personal protective equipment (PPE)** to use, whether the spill carries an **inhalation or explosion risk**, **decontamination procedures**, and **emergency telephone numbers**.
Have the labels and SDSs well organized and **alphabetically arranged by product name** to allow quick access in the event of a spill.
Always carry a **spill kit** with the items you will need to handle a spill during transport.
The contents of a spill kit are discussed in Chapter 9.
Inspect containers to ensure they have **legible and attached labels**, **tight closures**, and **pesticide-free outside surfaces**.
Secure application equipment, such as hand sprayers, backpack sprayers, and spreaders, during transport.
Protect pesticides from **extreme temperature and moisture** during transit.
Depending on the pesticide, **either extremely low or extremely high temperatures** can alter the stability of certain pesticide formulations.

figures.title: Always secure the load and carry in the truck a spill kit that includes a broom and shovel.
Pesticides stored incorrectly with feed, seed, and fertilizers increase the risk of contaminating non-pesticide products.

questions.q: Who does the manual say is the first person who can contain a spill during transport?
questions.why: The driver is the first person who can contain the spill and prevent it from spreading.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as SDS information that helps after a spill?
choices: Whether the spill carries an inhalation or explosion risk
The retail price of the product
questions.why: The SDS lists PPE, inhalation or explosion risk, decontamination procedures, and emergency phone numbers.

questions.q: A driver for a pest control company spills a pesticide on the highway. Who is accountable for injuries to people and the release into the environment?
choices: The driver and/or the owner of the company
No one, if it was an accident
questions.why: The person driving and/or the owner of the company is accountable.

questions.q: Only extremely high temperatures, not low temperatures, can alter the stability of pesticide formulations.
questions.why: Either extremely low or extremely high temperatures can alter stability, depending on the pesticide.

questions.q: According to the photo caption, what two tools should the truck's spill kit include?
questions.why: The caption says to carry a spill kit that includes a broom and shovel.

sections.title: Vehicle placards and the transportation security plan

p: DOT requires diamond-shaped signs called **placards** to be placed on vehicles that transport certain types and quantities of hazardous materials.
Most **distributors** will give you any required placards to place on your transportation vehicle.
Hazardous materials include some pesticides, fertilizers such as **anhydrous ammonia or ammonium nitrate**, and fuels such as **gasoline, diesel, and propane**.
Placards provide emergency responders with the information necessary to **quickly assess an accident situation**.
If you ship or transport materials in quantities that require placards, you must develop and implement a **transportation security plan**.
Vehicles must be placarded when transporting pesticides in any of these ways.

list: Bearing a **DOT poison label**.
In containers **larger than 119 gallons**.
In quantities **greater than 1,000 pounds**.

p: The security plan must include measures to **prevent unauthorized access**, a **security check of employees** who pick up and transport placarded hazardous materials, and the **intended route of travel**.
For further details on the transportation security plan, contact the **Hazardous Materials Information Center**.

figures.title: Examples of placards placed on vehicles that transport certain types of hazardous materials.
explain: The six example placards are: Dangerous 4, Gasoline 3, Oxidizer 5.1, Poison 6, Inhalation Hazard 2, and Flammable 3.
Each one is a diamond-shaped sign with the hazard name and a number.

questions.q: Vehicles must be placarded when transporting pesticides in containers larger than how many gallons?
questions.why: Placards are required for containers larger than 119 gallons.

questions.q: Vehicles must be placarded when transporting pesticides in quantities greater than how many pounds?
questions.why: Placards are required for quantities greater than 1,000 pounds.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a required part of a transportation security plan?
choices: A security check of employees who transport placarded hazardous materials
A copy of each employee's driving record from the last 10 years
questions.why: The plan covers unauthorized access, employee security checks, and the intended route of travel.

questions.q: You will haul 1,500 pounds of a pesticide. What must you develop and implement?
questions.why: Quantities that require placards also require a transportation security plan.

questions.q: Who does the manual say will give you any required placards?
questions.why: Most distributors will give you any required placards.

sections.title: Storage buildings, site security, and water damage

p: Although existing buildings are often used for pesticide storage, it is best to have a **separate storage facility** for pesticides, fertilizers, and other similar products.
Storing pesticides separately gives emergency response crews **more options in dealing with fires and spills**.
Keeping **equipment, employees, and records away from pesticides** is always recommended where possible.
A well-designed pesticide storage site does the following.

list: **Limits access.**
Permits better **inventory control**.
Protects people from exposure.
Reduces the chance of environmental contamination.
Prevents damage to pesticides from **temperature extremes and excess moisture**.
Safeguards pesticides from **theft, vandalism, and unauthorized use**.
Allows **fire departments to know the location** of products.

p: Whether the designated storage area is a **cabinet, an entire room, or a separate building**, **keep it locked when not in use**.
**Post warning signs on doors and windows** to alert others that pesticides are stored inside.
Pesticide security is covered in detail later in this chapter.
Pesticide storage facilities should **not be located in a flood zone**.
Carefully consider **soil and land surface characteristics** when selecting a storage site to prevent contamination of surface water or groundwater.
Do not locate the storage facility **near a stream likely to flood** or where **runoff water flows toward the facility**.
If flooding is likely, consider **building dikes** around the storage facility.
Work with local **zoning and building code professionals** to determine how best to protect the environment if high water were to enter the storage facility.
Consider storing pesticides on a **raised pallet or on shelves** to prevent high water from damaging pesticide containers or flowing water from moving them offsite.
Water or excess moisture may damage pesticide containers and their contents and cause the following.

list: **Metal containers to rust.**
**Paper and cardboard containers to split or crumble.**
Pesticide labeling to peel, smear, or otherwise become unreadable.
Dry pesticides to clump, degrade, or dissolve.
Slow-release products to release their active ingredients.

figures.title: Maintain a well designed, secure pesticide storage facility with highly visible warning signs. Keep it well ventilated and located where water damage is not likely to occur.
Do not store pesticides in locations that can become damp or wet.

questions.q: Which statement about pesticide storage facilities is true?
choices: A ventilation system may reduce noxious vapors by venting air into an adjoining area.
Carefully consider the terrain when selecting a storage site.
The floor should remain as bare soil to absorb any spilled material.
questions.why: Consider soil and land surface characteristics. Venting to an adjoining room does little, and floors should be impervious.

questions.q: Why does the manual say it is best to store pesticides in a separate facility?
choices: It gives emergency response crews more options in dealing with fires and spills
It is required for all private applicators
questions.why: Separate storage gives emergency crews more options with fires and spills.

questions.q: Your company stores pesticides in a single locked cabinet, not a building. What does the manual say about securing it?
choices: A cabinet does not need to be locked
Keep it locked when not in use and post warning signs
Only rooms and buildings need signs
questions.why: Whether a cabinet, room, or building, keep it locked when not in use and post warning signs.

questions.q: Where does the manual say to post warning signs at a pesticide storage site?
questions.why: Post warning signs on doors and windows.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as damage that water or excess moisture may cause?
choices: Dry pesticides to clump, degrade, or dissolve
Slow-release products to release their active ingredients
questions.why: Freezing is not on the moisture list.

questions.q: If flooding is likely at a storage site, what does the manual say to consider building?
choices: A drainage ditch to the nearest stream
questions.why: If flooding is likely, consider building dikes around the facility.

sections.title: Ventilation, lighting, floors, and what belongs in storage

p: Choose a **well-ventilated room where temperatures are controlled**.
**Exhaust fans directed to the outside** of the building reduce the buildup of noxious vapors from many of the solvents used in pesticide formulations.
**Ventilating the pesticide storage room into an adjoining room does little to solve the problem.**
Pesticide labeling often gives **temperature limits** for storing a product.
Consider installing an exhaust fan **on a timer** to automatically turn on at a certain temperature.
If the exhaust fan is not on a timer, **turn on the fan switch before entering** the storage room.
**Wait a few minutes** to allow any vapors to clear.
Be sure the pesticide storage facility is **well-lighted**.
Pesticide handlers entering the building must be able to **read the product labels** and determine whether **containers are leaking**.
Use **cement or other impervious materials** for flooring to retain the spilled material on the surface.
Such surfaces are easy to clean and decontaminate in the event of a release.
A floor that **slopes into a sump** helps collect and contain the spill.
Consider using shelving and pallets made of **nonabsorbent materials, such as plastic or metal**, for the same reasons as impervious floors.
Store **only pesticide containers, pesticide equipment, and a spill cleanup kit** at the storage site.

Keep **food, drink, tobacco, feed, medication, medical or veterinary supplies, seed (treated and untreated), clothing, and PPE** (other than that necessary for emergency response) out of the storage location.
Store pesticide containers with the **labels in plain sight**.
Costly errors may result if the wrong pesticide is chosen.
Be sure labels are always legible.

If the label is destroyed or damaged, **immediately mark the container** with some basic labeling information, such as the **trade name, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) registration number, signal word, and use classification**.
Go online to find a product replacement label or get a **new label from the manufacturer**.

figures.title: Be sure the floor of the pesticide containment site is made of non-porous materials such as sealed cement. A recessed floor helps control spills or leaking pesticides.

questions.q: Where should exhaust fans in a pesticide storage room be directed?
choices: To the outside of the building
questions.why: Fans directed to the outside reduce noxious vapor buildup. An adjoining room does little.

questions.q: The storage room's exhaust fan is not on a timer. What should you do before going in?
choices: Open a window after you are inside
Turn on the fan switch before entering, then wait a few minutes for vapors to clear
Hold your breath and work quickly
questions.why: Turn on the fan before entering and wait a few minutes for vapors to clear.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a recommended material for a storage floor or shelving?
questions.why: The manual calls for cement or other impervious flooring and nonabsorbent shelving such as plastic or metal.

questions.q: Which of these does the manual say SHOULD be stored at the pesticide storage site?
questions.why: Store only pesticide containers, pesticide equipment, and a spill cleanup kit.

questions.q: A label on a jug in storage has torn off and is unreadable. What should you do first?
choices: Immediately mark the container with basic labeling information such as trade name, EPA registration number, signal word, and use classification
Pour it into a labeled container of a similar product
questions.why: Immediately mark the container with basic labeling information, then get a replacement label.

p: Store pesticides in their **original containers** or, if allowed by state law, in a **properly labeled service container**.
Never use any other container to store a product.
Besides being illegal, serious injury may result when using **food containers, such as milk jugs or soft drink bottles**.
Children will associate the shape, size, and color of the container with its usual contents.
Never use a pesticide product from an unmarked or unlabeled container unless you are certain what it is.
Guessing wrong can cause serious damage at the application site.
Keep pesticide containers **securely closed** when not in use.
Just like bagged fertilizer, **dry pesticide formulations can clump** together under high humidity.
Consider placing partially used bags of wettable and soluble powders, dry flowables, dusts, and granules in a **plastic trash bag or tub with a cover** to reduce clumping.
Place **drums and bags on plastic pallets**.
Store other pesticides on **metal shelving**, placing the **heaviest containers on lower shelves**.
Do not allow containers to **extend beyond the edge of the shelving**. They could be knocked off or torn open.
Place **bulk and mini-bulk tanks on a reinforced concrete pad**.
**Diking** around bulk tanks keeps leaking pesticides inside a contained area.
Make the area inside a dike large enough to contain **the volume of the liquid in the tank plus at least an additional 10%**.
Keep **valves and pumps as well as transfer hoses within the diked area** when not in use.
Contact your state, tribe, or territory pesticide regulatory agency for guidance on what constitutes bulk pesticides and to learn specific rules for building containment structures.

figures.title: Do not store pesticides in food containers.
Store pesticides on metal shelving, with the heaviest containers and liquids stored on the lower shelves. Never extend beyond the edge of the shelving.

questions.q: How large should the area inside a dike around a bulk tank be?
choices: Equal to the volume of the liquid in the tank
The volume of the liquid in the tank plus at least an additional 10%
Twice the volume of the tank
The volume of the tank plus 119 gallons
questions.why: The dike must hold the tank's liquid volume plus at least an additional 10%.

questions.q: A coworker pours leftover insecticide into an empty soft drink bottle to store it. What does the manual say?
choices: That is fine if the cap is tight
It is illegal and can cause serious injury, because people associate the container with its usual contents
It is fine if the bottle is stored up high
It is fine for less than a week
questions.why: Using food containers is illegal and may cause serious injury.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a correct storage practice from the manual?
choices: Place drums and bags on plastic pallets
Place the heaviest containers on lower shelves
Let containers extend past the shelf edge to save space
Place bulk tanks on a reinforced concrete pad
questions.why: Containers must not extend beyond the shelf edge, where they could be knocked off or torn open.

questions.q: Valves, pumps, and transfer hoses for a bulk tank should be kept within the diked area when not in use.
questions.why: Keep valves, pumps, and transfer hoses within the diked area when not in use.

questions.q: What does the manual suggest putting partially used bags of dry formulations in to reduce clumping?
questions.answer: a plastic trash bag or tub with a cover
questions.why: A plastic trash bag or tub with a cover reduces clumping.

sections.title: Damaged containers, shelf life, and safety tips

p: Regularly inspect pesticide containers to detect problems at the outset.
If you find a damaged container, **put on appropriate PPE** and **place it into a larger container, such as a 5-gallon bucket**.
Clean up spilled pesticide and place any contaminated materials in the bucket.
If possible, **use the pesticide immediately** on a site and at a rate allowed by the label, or **dispose of it according to label directions**.
Keep an **inventory** of all pesticides in storage, **marking each container or box with the year it was purchased**.
In this way, you can **use the oldest product first**.
Remember to use it as it was meant to be used. A replacement product may have different label directions and uses.
If you have questions about the shelf life of a product, contact the **dealer or manufacturer**.
Avoid storing large quantities of pesticides for long periods. **Buy only as much as you need for the season.**
For best results, do the following.
list: Have **duplicate copies of pesticide labels and SDSs** available in case of an emergency.
Wear appropriate protective clothing when handling pesticide containers.
**Label items such as measuring utensils and protective equipment** to prevent their use for other purposes.
Have **absorbent materials** readily available to soak up leaks in the storage room. Keep a **shovel, broom, and heavy-duty plastic bags** on hand to remove the contaminated absorbent material.
Check the **SDS** for materials that will **deactivate a contaminated surface**. When in doubt, contact the pesticide manufacturer for a recommendation.

p: Have readily accessible **clean water for decontamination, an eyewash station, personal protective equipment, a fire extinguisher rated for chemical fires, first aid equipment, and emergency telephone numbers**.
Additionally, keep plenty of **soap, water, and paper towels** available near the storage facility.

figures.title: Place damaged pesticide containers in secondary containment.
Mark each container with its purchase date.

questions.q: What is the first thing to do if a pesticide container is leaking?
questions.why: If you find a damaged container, put on appropriate PPE first.

questions.q: Which recommended practice will minimize pesticide storage problems?
choices: Purchase quantities based on previous usage.
Purchase more than you need to ensure availability of the product.
Store metal pesticide containers on the higher shelves to prevent rusting.
questions.ref: pp. 126 and 128, 'Prevent Water Damage' and 'Note Shelf Life of Pesticides' (Appendix A: C)
questions.why: The manual's answer key (Appendix A) gives this answer. The chapter text as typed does not clearly back it up, so it is flagged for a re-check against the answer key page.

questions.q: Why should you mark each container or box with the year it was purchased?
choices: So you can use the oldest product first
So you can return it for a refund
So the fire department knows its age
questions.why: Marking the purchase year lets you use the oldest product first.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT on the manual's list of things to keep readily accessible near pesticide storage?
choices: A fire extinguisher rated for chemical fires
A garden hose connected to a storm drain
questions.why: The list includes clean water, an eyewash station, PPE, a chemical-rated extinguisher, first aid, and emergency numbers.

questions.q: You find a cracked jug in storage and have put on PPE. What do you do with the jug?
choices: Place it into a larger container, such as a 5-gallon bucket
Pour it down the floor drain
Tape the crack and put it back
Leave it for the next inspection
questions.why: Place it into a larger container, such as a 5-gallon bucket, and clean up the spill.

questions.q: Where should you check to find materials that will deactivate a contaminated surface?
questions.why: Check the SDS. When in doubt, contact the manufacturer.

p: **Do not accumulate outdated or unwanted pesticide products.**
Not only will you lose money by not using the product, but you may have to **pay a disposal service**.
If you **use the product up according to the label**, you will avoid both problems.
Sometimes **EPA will cancel a product registration**.
When this occurs, EPA usually either **allows the continued use of the product until it has cleared the distribution chain** or **issues a federal notice prohibiting use after a specific date**.
If you keep such products after that date, you may have to **dispose of them as hazardous waste**.
Be sure to **follow label directions for disposal** of any excess or leftover product.
If you are holding pesticides or emptied pesticide containers for disposal or recycling, keep them in a **special section of the storage area**.
See Chapter 10 (Planning the Pesticide Application) for information on pesticide container rinsing procedures.
Some states sponsor **pesticide disposal programs** that collect unwanted pesticides from growers and applicators **free or at reduced cost**.
Contact your state, tribe, or territory pesticide regulatory agency to see if a program is available in your area.

figures.title: Have a designated area for properly rinsed containers.

questions.q: When EPA cancels a product registration, what does EPA usually do?
choices: Orders all stocks destroyed within 24 hours
Either allows use until the product clears the distribution chain or issues a federal notice prohibiting use after a specific date
questions.why: EPA usually allows use until the product clears the distribution chain, or bans use after a specific date.

questions.q: You still have a canceled pesticide after EPA's prohibition date. What may you have to do?
choices: Dispose of it as hazardous waste
Dilute it and pour it out
questions.why: Products kept past that date may have to be disposed of as hazardous waste.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT something the manual says about a buildup of unwanted pesticides?
choices: You lose money by not using the product
You may have to pay a disposal service
Old pesticides become more toxic every year
Using it up according to the label avoids both problems
questions.why: The manual cites lost money and disposal costs, not rising toxicity.

questions.q: Pesticides and empty containers held for disposal or recycling should be kept in a special section of the storage area.
questions.why: Keep them in a special section of the storage area.

questions.q: Who should you contact to learn whether a pesticide disposal program is available in your area?
questions.answer: your state, tribe, or territory pesticide regulatory agency
questions.why: Contact your state, tribe, or territory pesticide regulatory agency.

sections.title: Pesticide site security and risk assessment

p: Minimizing risks for the safety of employees, customers, and communities should always be a top priority when it comes to storing pesticides.
Every pesticide storage facility should examine its security efforts and **plan for worst-case scenarios**.
Routinely review your security measures to determine whether all risks have been accounted for in the plan.
Without effective security procedures, you may be vulnerable to both **internal (employee theft)** and **external (terrorism, theft, and vandalism)** threats.
This puts both employees and the community at risk.
By developing a strong and workable security plan, managers, employees, and emergency responders can reduce the likelihood of theft or other mishaps.
In addition, effective security avoids costly losses.
An incident of any magnitude can seriously disrupt operations and result in lawsuits, costly remediation actions, employee fear and uncertainty, and damage to the company's reputation.
A well-planned security program can do the following.

list: Safeguard employees and the community.
Maintain the integrity of operations.
**Reduce insurance costs.**
Prevent theft.
Reduce vandalism and sabotage.
Protect confidential business information.
Improve relationships with local authorities and community leaders.

p: **The first step in developing a security program is to conduct a risk assessment** of your business or farm's vulnerabilities.
Make a list of **assets that need protecting, possible threats, and steps** that can be taken to protect them.
Any place that stores or transports pesticides shares similar assets, which are broadly defined as **people, information, and property**.
"People" includes employees, visitors, customers, contractors, and neighbors.
"Information" includes business, proprietary, and employee material deemed confidential.
"Property" may include the following.

list: Pesticide storage facilities.
Vehicles.
Application equipment.
Bulk storage tanks.
Mixing and loading sites.
All utilities, such as telephone, water, gas, and electric.

figures.title: Be sure to guard against unauthorized entry.

questions.q: What is the first step a business should take to develop an effective pesticide security program?
choices: Conduct a risk assessment of business vulnerabilities.
questions.why: The first step in developing a security program is a risk assessment.

questions.q: The manual broadly defines the assets of any place that stores or transports pesticides as which three things?
questions.why: Assets are broadly defined as people, information, and property.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed as a benefit of a well-planned security program?
choices: Eliminate the need for a pesticide license
questions.why: Security does not replace licensing. The other three are on the list.

questions.q: An employee steals pesticides from the storage building. What kind of threat is this, according to the manual?
questions.why: Internal threats are employee theft. External threats are terrorism, theft, and vandalism.

questions.q: Under the manual's definition, neighbors count as part of the "people" asset.
questions.why: People includes employees, visitors, customers, contractors, and neighbors.

p: Train employees to be **vigilant in detecting security threats**.
Employees are familiar with what occurs in and around a pesticide storage facility or at the job site.
They can provide an **early warning** when something seems out of place or someone is acting suspiciously.
At a minimum, instruct all employees on **pesticide inventory control, security of storage facilities and application equipment, and emergency preparedness and response**.
Fundamental security tasks include the following.
**Secure buildings, manufacturing facilities, storage areas, and surrounding property.**
Prevent the unauthorized entry of persons into areas used to manufacture or store pesticides.
Elements of an effective security plan may range from **log sheets, identification badges, fencing, lighting, and locks** to **detection systems, cameras, and trained guards**.
**Secure pesticide application equipment and vehicles.**
Keep unauthorized people away from equipment used for storing, mixing, loading, transferring, transporting, and applying pesticides.
Secure and disable equipment in the field to prevent misuse.
For example, **do not leave keys in the ignition**, and lock doors and cabinets.
**Reclaim keys from employees when they terminate employment.**

figures.title: Outside lights on a pesticide storage building help prevent theft and vandalism.
Lock backpack sprayers securely onto the transport vehicle.

questions.q: Which of the following is considered a good security practice?
choices: Instruct employees on pesticide inventory control.
Back up confidential data daily and keep it at the facility.
questions.why: At a minimum, instruct all employees on pesticide inventory control.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the minimum topics to instruct all employees on?
choices: Security of storage facilities and application equipment
questions.why: The minimum topics are inventory control, security, and emergency preparedness and response.

sections.title: Security procedures, authorities, and prevention steps

p: **Protect confidential information.**
As safety and security systems become more reliant on computers and other technology, it is important to secure them from hackers and intruders.
Such efforts include **contingency planning for power disruptions, adherence to password and backup procedures**, and other measures to ensure that only authorized personnel have access.
**Develop procedures and policies that support security needs.**
Recommended practices include effective **hiring and labor policies, inventory management, and planning for emergencies**.
Hiring and labor policies should include **employee training, background checks, and workplace violence prevention**.
Inventory management is necessary to keep track of pesticides stored at the facility.
Planning for emergency response is critical. It helps to ensure that managers and employees know how to respond in the unlikely event of pesticide release, bomb threat, or terrorist activity.
**Coordinate with authorities in a timely manner.**
If you believe a security breach or suspicious activity has occurred, **contact local authorities immediately**.
In addition to alerting the police department, call the **local emergency planning commission, fire departments**, and other emergency response agencies.

The **Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)** cautions that any suspicious activity related to the use, training, or acquisition of pesticides should be immediately reported to management and local authorities.
To minimize risks, do the following.
list: Adopt security measures to deter tampering with chemicals, equipment, or the facility itself.
Include local authorities, for example police and firefighters, in developing the security plan.
Keep an accurate inventory of all chemicals.
Keep chemical storage areas locked when not in use.
Update your emergency response plan and practice the procedures.
Post telephone numbers of law enforcement and emergency response agencies in a prominent location.
Be cautious of **unknown persons who want to pay cash for large quantities** of pesticides.
Ask employees to report any unusual incidents or requests.
Restrict access of nonemployees to your pesticide storage facilities.

choices: Sell it; cash sales are safest
Be cautious of unknown persons who want to pay cash for large quantities of pesticides
Require them to show a driver license only

questions.why: Hiring and labor policies include training, background checks, and workplace violence prevention.

questions.why: Include local authorities in developing the security plan.

questions.answer: the local emergency planning commission or fire departments
questions.why: Also call the local emergency planning commission, fire departments, and other emergency response agencies.

p: It is essential to establish safety and security practices for moving pesticides on the highways and at storage and job sites.
Because spills and accidents are **more likely to occur while transporting or applying pesticides**, drivers and pesticide applicators must be **trained to respond quickly to a spill**.
**Pesticide labels and SDSs** for the pesticide carried in the vehicle can provide important information in the event of a spill.
Attention to pesticide site security and managing pesticides should be a **top priority**.
Develop **security and emergency management plans** for every pesticide-handling and storage facility to safeguard employees and the community.
Design security plans to reduce the risk of **theft, vandalism, and deliberate misuse** of pesticides by those wanting to harm others.
Train employees in security and emergency response procedures and to coordinate efforts with **local police, emergency response personnel, and the FBI**.

questions.why: Spills and accidents are more likely while transporting or applying pesticides.
